newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols flat as spot commutes in ranges.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols flat as spot commutes in ranges.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were barely changed in U.S. business as spot commuted back down to the middle of recent ranges after Thursday's bounce, dealers said.

They noted that, despite the weekend time-decay pressure, they have had enough spot movement lately to painlessly hold on to their short-dated positions built up for Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
"You probably can pay up a little bit for gamma just because you are getting nice (spot) movements," said Ted Voorhees, a senior trader at Deutsche Bank in New York.
Shorter-dated options have higher gamma, which gives them quick price acceleration against spot market gyration but also makes them vulnerable to time decay.
Voorhees said buying interest in the short-dates focused on Wednesday and Thursday expiries, while Monday and Tuesday expiries were under pressure.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark stood at 9.9/10.1 percent at U.S. midsession, virtually unchanged from late Thursday levels.
One-month dollar/yen volatility stood at 10.3/10.5 percent, up 0.1 point on the day.

The dollar, which had become bullish on Thursday after hawkish comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, tumbled today after reports that Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin said excess dollar strength was not good for the U.S. economy.

"Risk reversals two days ago were for dollar downside, coming in this morning (they were) for dollar upside, and now I just made one (deal) around par," Voorhees said. Risk reversals reflect the cost of swapping equally out-of-the-money puts and calls.
He suggested back end options might not be worth holding as such daily directional flips kept spot range-bound.

"I don't think you can really afford to be long vega," he said. It is generally difficult to cash in profit from intraday spot fluctuations by delta-hedging longer-dated options, which have higher vega but relatively low gamma.
That could be one reason why the back end has lagged the rise in the rest of the dollar/mark curve this week, Voorhees said. One-year dollar/mark stood steady at 9.9/10.1 percent.

On the other hand, other traders still saw value in longer-dateds, particularly in dollar/yen, as the strong up moves in the dollar in the early part of the year could resume or sharply reverse any time.
An interbank broker said there was a big buyer in six-month and one-year 10-delta strangles today.
"There was strong buying in back-date low-delta strangles, something worth talking about," he said.

Such low-delta strangles tend to be more sensitive to volatility than their present vega levels suggest because they become less out-of-the-money in delta terms when volatility rises, even if spot did not move very much. Interbank dealers, generally short the outside strikes because of their sales to end-users, have been suffering from such stagnant spot/higher volatility scenario.
